payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
The first licensing deals between major labels and AI music companies closed in late 2025, and they changed who has to make the next decision. A label can license a catalog, but the individual artist still has to decide whether to opt in. That invitation now arrives in ordinary inboxes, usually as an email and a dashboard with a revenue share attached.

I've worked on roughly 110 releases since 2022, and I have my own catalog to think about. This is the procedure I'd follow before saying yes to any of these offers. It assumes no legal training, only patience and a willingness to ask direct questions.

Read the scope before the rate

The rate is the most visible number in the offer, which is exactly why it should be read last. Start with what the platform wants to do with the music. Many offers bundle two different uses, and they deserve separate answers.

A · Training

The model learns from your recordings

Your catalog becomes part of what a general model learned from. Nobody can ask for you by name, and the output rarely points back to any single contributor.

B · Voice or style on request

Users can ask for you by name

The platform offers your voice or style as a selectable option, which puts your identity inside the product, not only your recordings.

An artist can reasonably accept one and refuse the other. Some offers describe the use in language broad enough to cover anything the company builds later, and the courts are still working out what training on a catalog actually costs the people in it. If the agreement doesn't say plainly which recordings are included and what they're used for, the honest reading is that it covers everything.

Write down, in your own words, what you think you're granting. If you can't, you have your first question for the platform.

Ask how the money is counted, then how you leave

A percentage means little until you know what it's a percentage of and who does the counting. Find out whether payment tracks how much your work is used or gets split evenly across everyone who opted in. Then ask whether you'll ever see the underlying numbers, or only a total. A share you can't check is a share you take on faith every quarter.

Credit belongs in the same conversation. When the system generates something that leans on your contribution, does anything in the output or its listing name you? Plenty of offers are silent here, and silence usually means no.

The exit comes last. If you withdraw in a year, what happens to the model that already learned from your work, and to the payments tied to it? Consent you can't take back is closer to a sale. Selling is fine, as long as the price reflects it.

Keep your own copy

An artist does not need to understand how a model is trained to decide whether to join one. They need the terms in writing, in plain language, before anything is used: which works, for what purpose, from what date, and at what rate. They also need a copy that belongs to them, rather than a page that lives only inside the platform. A dashboard is the platform's account of itself, and it can change without notice.

The practical test is simple. Could your manager, or a lawyer you trust, read the agreement in ten minutes and explain back exactly what you granted and how you get out? If explaining it takes a call to the platform's support team, wait. The offer won't disappear while you hold off, and by then someone else may have asked the same questions in public.

payload.title: Before you opt in to an AI music platform
